questions.question: Q: Why is the Cenozoic called the 'Age of Mammals'?

points.text: After the K-Pg extinction eliminated the dinosaurs (~66 Ma), mammals rapidly diversified to fill the vacant ecological niches. They evolved from small, nocturnal creatures into the wide variety of forms we see today, including whales, horses, primates and elephants.

questions.question: Q: What caused the repeated glacial-interglacial cycles of the Pleistocene?

points.text: Milankovitch cycles: variations in Earth's orbital parameters (eccentricity of orbit, tilt of axis, and precession of equinoxes) that alter the distribution and intensity of solar radiation received at different latitudes over tens of thousands of years.

questions.question: Q: How did glaciation shape the British landscape?

points.text: Glaciers carved U-shaped valleys (e.g. Lake District), corries (cwms) on mountainsides, and arêtes. They deposited till (boulder clay) as moraines and drumlins. Erratics were carried far from their source. Meltwater channels and eskers were formed by glacial rivers. Glacial lakes deposited varved clays.

questions.question: Q: What is an erratic and what does it tell us?

points.text: A rock fragment transported by a glacier and deposited on different bedrock from its origin. Erratics indicate the direction of ice flow (tracing them to their source outcrop) and the maximum extent of ice sheets.

questions.question: Q: Why did sea level change during the ice ages?

points.text: During glacial periods, water was stored on land as ice sheets, causing sea level to fall by ~120 m. During interglacials, the ice melted and returned to the oceans, raising sea level. This is eustatic sea level change. Britain was connected to Europe by a land bridge during low sea levels.
